questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutions of a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the body that made binding decisions inside the regional project.
questions.stem: Tonight's revision starts with a table of the regional project's institutions; which body was empowered to take binding decisions inside it?

options.text: A permanent executive appointed by the governments of the member states, with a fixed term of office.
A rotating chair drawn from the member states, which acted only as a coordinator of votes.
options.misconception: mistakes a chairmanship for a decision-making body

options.text: An assembly of national parliamentarians, which debated policy without deciding anything.
options.misconception: believes the assembly was the decision-maker

options.text: A standing secretariat in a neutral city, which issued guidance on the treaty but not decisions.
options.misconception: treats a secretariat as the governing body

questions.explanation: The table shows a permanent executive with a fixed term and powers of its own, which is what distinguished the project from a simple treaty between governments. The assembly and the chair had consultative roles only.
questions.hint: Look for the row with a fixed term of office.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A regional treaty's text
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the treaty's text bound the member states.
questions.stem: The revision sheet asks the group to explain how a treaty could bind states that had retained their own governments.

answer.exemplar: The binding came from what the text took away and what it created. It took away the right of each member to set its own external tariff, and replaced a set of separate tariffs with one common rate applied by the shared executive, so that no member could undercut the others by lowering duties. It created a common court to which the member governments themselves were subject, and a common body in which they were outnumbered and outvoted. Power thus moved upwards into institutions the members themselves financed and staffed, and the treaty made that transfer irreversible in the sense that leaving would mean dismantling everything that had been built on top of it.

questions.explanation: The treaty removed each government's control of its external tariff, created a court the members were subject to, and set up institutions where they could be outvoted. That is how it bound states that kept their own governments.
questions.hint: Think about what the text took away from members.

questions.topic: Why a regional project appears

stimulus.body: A note on the origins of a regional project records that the states involved had just fought a war across their own borders, that two of them feared for their security and one had lost much of its industrial base, and that a shared administration of a heavy industry was proposed because none of the parties trusted the others to disarm in the ordinary way.

questions.stem: During the session, a card quotes the reasons the founders gave for the project; what did the note identify as the underlying cause?

options.text: A desire for a common currency to simplify the movement of goods between neighbours.
Fear that the old rivalry would return unless the heavy industry was put under shared control.
The wish to create a single overseas colony administered for the whole group.
A shortage of officials trained to administer the territories they had inherited.

questions.explanation: The note links the project to security: the founders did not trust one another to disarm, so a shared administration of the heavy industry seemed safer than rival armament. The other motives are not in the note.
questions.hint: Look for the fear expressed in the note.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule set aside inside a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the rule that was set aside within the regional project.

stimulus.body: A decision rule note records that the founding treaty required every decision of the council of governments to be taken unanimously, and that a later amending treaty replaced that requirement for a specified list of subjects, on which a qualified majority of the members by weighted votes was to suffice. The note adds that the heaviest members were given larger votes than the smaller ones.

questions.stem: The group's notes on the suspended rule identify which change was made to the original decision procedure?

options.text: The rule was kept, but a casting vote was given to the chair of the council of governments.
options.misconception: invents a casting vote for the chair

options.text: Unanimity was extended to every decision, including those previously taken by simple majority.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change

options.text: The requirement was dropped entirely, so that a simple majority of members decided everything.
options.misconception: claims ordinary majority voting replaced unanimity

options.text: Unanimity was replaced by a qualified majority of weighted votes on a named list of subjects.

questions.explanation: The note shows unanimity being replaced for a named list of subjects by a qualified majority of weighted votes. The rule was therefore set aside selectively rather than abolished, and no casting vote was created.
questions.hint: Compare the two sets of voting rules.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the end of a superpower did not change
questions.learningObjective: Identify what survived the end of a superpower unchanged.
questions.stem: In the revision, one member asks what the end of a superpower left entirely intact; explain why the framework survived.

answer.exemplar: The framework survived because it had been written to stand above the states that created it and to bind whoever came after them. The founding text made no provision for the dissolution of a member and did not need one: the obligations were attached to the organisation and the seat was attached to the state, not to the government that had exercised it. When one of the two superpowers came apart, its seat passed to a successor that accepted the existing rules as they stood, including the right of any permanent member to block substantive decisions. Nothing in the text had to be redrawn, and the practical effect was that the structure of the post-war settlement carried on with one fewer rival in it.

questions.explanation: The founding text bound successors as well as founders and tied the seat to the state rather than to a government, so a dissolution needed no amendment. The structure simply carried on with one fewer rival inside it.
questions.hint: Think about who the text was written to bind.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule set aside inside a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a rule inside the regional project was set aside.
questions.stem: The study group reads the rule on the assembly's membership; explain how that rule was set aside and why it mattered.

answer.exemplar: The founding treaty provided that members of the assembly would be appointed by the national parliaments and would serve as delegates of those parliaments. That was set aside by an amendment which allowed the assembly to be elected directly by the people of each member state, the first such elections being held in 1979. The reason lay in the weakness of the old arrangement. Delegates sent by parliaments could not speak for their constituents directly, so the assembly's claim to be a democratic voice was always arguable, and governments found it convenient to keep it that way. Direct election made the assembly the only part of the project elected by citizens, which changed how much weight its opinion carried and gave the project a public face of its own.

questions.explanation: The rule that assembly members be delegated by national parliaments was set aside by direct election, because delegated members could not claim to speak for the people. It gave the assembly a mandate that governments could not easily dismiss.
questions.hint: Think about who appoints the members of that body now.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutions of a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the regional project's institutions differed from a simple council of governments.
questions.stem: The revision sheet counts the institutions of the regional project; explain how they differed from a council of governments that could only pass recommendations.

answer.exemplar: A council of governments can only make recommendations, because every decision belongs to the member states and each of them must agree. The project's institutions were built to remove that dependence. The executive was given powers of its own and applied the common rules, including the common external tariff, so that compliance did not depend on the goodwill of national administrations. The court could rule against a member government and have its judgment enforced through the executive's own machinery. And the weighted voting arrangement meant that a group of smaller members could outvote the largest ones on many questions, so the institutions were not simply a larger version of the member governments sitting in conference. The result was a system in which decisions were taken without unanimity and could be enforced without national consent.

questions.explanation: The institutions took decisions without unanimity and enforced them without national consent, through an executive with its own powers and a court that could rule against members. That is the difference from a body that can only recommend.
questions.hint: Think about who applied the rules and who enforced the judgments.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A permanent seat after a superpower dissolved
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the seat's succession was not treated as a new membership.
questions.stem: During revision, the tutor asks how the seat was treated after the superpower dissolved; explain why the succession was not treated as a fresh application.

answer.exemplar: It was not treated as a fresh application because the founding text attached the seat to the state and not to the particular government holding the office at any moment. When that state broke up, the successor that carried on the state's international personality inherited the seat with it, and the letter of 1991 made the succession explicit so that no one could later argue that the seat had lapsed. Treating it as a new application would have been worse than merely inconvenient: it would have required a council recommendation and an assembly vote, and either organ could have refused, which would have left a vacancy in the permanent membership and handed the deciding vote to a different distribution of permanent members. The letter avoided that by asserting continuity and accepting the obligations that went with it.

questions.explanation: The founding text attached the seat to the state, so a successor inherited it rather than applying afresh. Treating it as a new application would have risked a vacancy in the permanent membership.
questions.hint: Think about which body would have had to vote.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a regional project appears
questions.learningObjective: Explain the economic reasoning behind the appearance of regional projects.
questions.stem: The group's notes on the project's early years suggest that its founders understood something about scale; explain what.

answer.exemplar: The founders understood that separate national economies could not hold their own against a much larger economy across the border. Each of the smaller states could be undercut on price by producers operating on a larger scale, and a national tariff could protect a domestic market only by making it dearer for the state's own firms, which were then less competitive abroad. Pooling the market solved both halves of that problem at once, since goods produced anywhere inside the group could move freely and the larger combined production base could compete with outsiders. The arithmetic also ran the other way: a shared administration of a heavy industry was easier for two neighbours who distrusted each other than an arms race, and it made them harder for a third power to divide.

questions.explanation: The founders saw that small national economies could not compete against a larger one beyond the border, and that a common market and a shared heavy industry solved that at once. Scale, not protection, was the reasoning.
questions.hint: Think about what a national tariff could and could not do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A letter about continuity
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the letter of continuity accomplished.
questions.stem: The revision pack's notes on the letter explain what the letter accomplished; explain why the step it took mattered so much.

answer.exemplar: The letter accomplished two things at once. It established, before anyone could raise the question, that the dissolved state had not ceased to be a member and that its seat had not fallen vacant, so that the permanent membership of the council remained five and the balance of power inside it remained as it had been. And it did so in a form that was easy to accept, because the same letter accepted the dissolved state's obligations in full, including its share of the cost of the organisation and its responsibility under every treaty to which the dissolved state had been party. A successor that wanted to argue for a fresh start would have had to argue for a fresh start without a seat, and nobody wanted that, so continuity was the obvious interest for everyone concerned.

questions.explanation: The letter confirmed continuity of membership, the seat and the obligations at once, so the permanent membership stayed at five and the settlement's balance held. Continuity was the interest of every party.
questions.hint: Think about what a vacancy in the permanent membership would mean.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the intervention required of members
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the intervention required of the members of the regional project.
questions.stem: The study group's timeline records that the members were told what they would have to do; explain why the requirements were drafted as obligations rather than as aspirations.

answer.exemplar: The requirements were drafted as obligations because aspirations had already been tried and had failed. Earlier declarations of friendship and shared intentions had been torn up within a generation, and the founders of the project understood that the only reliable test of an arrangement is whether it survives the first disagreement. So the text did not say that members ought to remove their duties on one another's goods; it said they would, and it named the body that would collect the common external tariff and the body that would hear a complaint about a failure to comply. Obligation plus enforcement was what made the difference between a project that could actually be run and a series of declarations that each side could abandon when it became inconvenient.

questions.explanation: Obligations with named bodies to enforce them made the arrangement survivable, where earlier declarations of goodwill had been torn up at the first disagreement. Enforceability was the point of the drafting.
questions.hint: Think about what happened to earlier declarations of goodwill.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A regional treaty's text
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the treaty's text allowed the project to develop beyond its original purpose.
questions.stem: The group's notes on the regional project explain how the treaty allowed the project to grow; explain how that was possible.

answer.exemplar: The treaty was drafted with a procedure for its own amendment, and the amendment clause was itself deliberately generous: a qualified majority of the members could revise the text without the unanimity that the original voting rule demanded, and the revision could add new tasks to the project as well as change existing ones. That combination is what allowed a project begun to manage one heavy industry to become a customs union, and then a common market with a common external tariff and rules on agricultural prices and competition. Each step was taken under the amended voting rule, so the founders locked the direction of the project into the text without locking its scope, and the institutions could keep up with the tasks they were given.

questions.explanation: A generous amendment clause let the members revise the text by qualified majority and add new tasks, so the project's scope could grow while its direction stayed fixed. That is how it outgrew its original purpose.
questions.hint: Think about how a treaty can change itself.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the end of a superpower did not change
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the organisation's foundations were untouched by the dissolution.
questions.stem: The group's notes explain that the veto survived the dissolution; explain why the founding text had been written in a way that allowed that.

answer.exemplar: The text was written in terms of states and offices rather than of particular governments and personalities, and it contained no clause allowing a seat to lapse. The duty to accept the council's decisions and the right to stop a substantive decision were both attached to the seat and to the state that held it, so both travelled with the successor when the state itself was continued. Because the text was addressed to states that had not yet existed when it was signed, it worked for the successors of those states as well. The result was that the framework could absorb the largest structural change of the century without amendment, which is the strongest evidence that it had been drafted as a set of procedures rather than as a settlement between particular governments.

questions.explanation: The text attached rights and duties to states and seats rather than to governments, and allowed no lapse, so both travelled to the successor. Written for states that had not yet existed, it bound their successors too.
questions.hint: Think about who the text addresses.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule set aside inside a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the regional project dealt with a rule that was set aside.
questions.stem: In tonight's pack, a summary of the treaty's rule is marked as set aside; explain how the project handled a rule that was no longer observed.

answer.exemplar: A rule that was no longer observed could not simply be ignored, because the whole point of the project was that its members could be held to it. So the project dealt with such a rule in two ways. If the rule had been overtaken by a later amendment, the amendment simply replaced it in the text, and the old wording was struck out so that the treaty said only one thing about the matter in question. If the rule had been quietly broken in practice, the executive's first move was to require an explanation and, if the answer was unsatisfactory, to open the procedure that could end with the member's rights in the institutions being suspended. Either way, the difference between a rule that had been replaced and a rule that had merely been breached was settled by looking at the text and at what the member had actually done.

questions.explanation: A rule that had been replaced was struck out by amendment, while a rule that had merely been breached was handled through the executive's procedure, ending in suspension. Text and conduct settled the difference.
questions.hint: Distinguish a replaced rule from a broken one.

questions.topic: What the intervention required of members
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the intervention required of the members of the regional project.

stimulus.body: An entry note records the conditions on which a state entered a regional project: it had to accede to the founding text and to each of the later amendments, to accept the common external tariff at its own frontiers, to give effect to the common rules in its own legislation within a stated period, to contribute to the common budget, and to accept the jurisdiction of the project's court over any dispute concerning the treaty.

questions.stem: The revision sheet asks what the superpower's end required of the organisation's members; what does the entry note show about entry in general?

options.text: That joining required only the payment of a subscription to a common fund.
That joining required legal obligations to be accepted in full, not a loose association.
That joining required a recommendation from the project's largest member.
options.misconception: invents a veto for the largest member

options.text: That joining could be provisional, with a trial period before obligations began.

questions.explanation: The note lists accession to the text, application of the common rules, budget contributions and acceptance of the court's jurisdiction, which together made entry a set of legal obligations. Nothing in it describes a subscription, a sponsor's approval or a trial period.
questions.hint: Read the list of conditions in order.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A permanent seat after a superpower dissolved
questions.learningObjective: Identify the instrument that settled the question of the permanent seat.

stimulus.body: An instrument note records that the question of the successor's seat was settled by correspondence rather than by decision, that the letter used was addressed to the organisation's secretary-general and notified to the members, and that the organisation treated the letter as sufficient notice of continuity and entered the successor in the membership accordingly.

questions.stem: A note in tonight's revision pack explains that the seat's succession was settled by what?

options.text: A decision of the council recorded in the minutes of a session held in January.
A resolution of the general assembly taken by a two-thirds majority of those present.
A letter to the secretary-general, treated as sufficient notice of continuity.
An agreement concluded at a meeting of the successor states themselves.

questions.explanation: The note shows the succession settled by correspondence: a letter to the secretary-general, treated as sufficient notice and entered in the membership records. No vote or decision by an organ was required.
questions.hint: Look at the form the settlement took.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the end of a superpower did not change
questions.learningObjective: Identify the arrangement that continued unchanged after the dissolution.
questions.stem: The group's notes identify what the end of a superpower left as the settlement's most durable element; which is it?

options.text: The practice of holding the assembly's session in the same city every year.
The practice of choosing the location of the organisation's headquarters by rotation.
The rule that the president of the assembly is chosen from the permanent members only.
The rule that substantive decisions require the permanent members' agreement, and one objection is enough.

questions.explanation: The requirement of the permanent members' agreement was the settlement's most durable element, because it sat in the founding text and required no amendment when a superpower ended. The other practices are not part of the arrangement.
questions.hint: Locate the rule that needed no amendment.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A letter about continuity
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of the letter about continuity.
questions.stem: The revision worksheet for the letter's consequences shows what result followed from it?

options.text: The permanent membership was enlarged, since the successor added a second permanent seat.
options.misconception: claims a second seat was added

options.text: The permanent membership of the council continued unchanged, and the seat was entered in the successor's name.
The council's size was reduced, since the seat was withdrawn and not replaced.
The organisation was suspended until the succession had been debated by all members.
options.misconception: invents a suspension of the organisation

questions.explanation: The worksheet shows the seat entered in the successor's name with no change to the number of permanent members. The letter added nothing to the council and withdrew nothing from it.
questions.hint: Compare the permanent membership before and after.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutions of a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the regional project's institutions included a body of national parliamentarians.
questions.stem: The tutor's revision notes record why the project included an assembly of national parliamentarians; explain what that body contributed.

answer.exemplar: The assembly existed because the executive and the council of governments alone would have left the project with no democratic element at all, and a project that pooled real powers over trade, industry and money could not be defended for long without one. Parliamentarians from the member states could scrutinise the budget and the executive's proposals, and they could carry the project back to their own electorates, where it was defended or criticised in public. That was the point of the body. Its weaknesses were equally clear, since members were seconded by national parliaments and answered to those parliaments rather than to the people who elected them, and it was eventually corrected by direct election, which is why the assembly's history reads as a long argument about who it represented and on what authority it spoke.

questions.explanation: The assembly gave the project a democratic element and a way to carry its decisions into national debate, which pooled powers over trade and money could not survive without. Its weak mandate was later corrected by direct election.
questions.hint: Think about what the body did for the project's legitimacy.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A regional treaty's text
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the treaty's text gave the project's institutions the power to do.

stimulus.body: A clause note records that the treaty instructed the executive to ensure the application of the common rules within the member states, to publish the decisions it took, to keep the accounts of the common institutions and to have them examined by an independent audit body, and to report annually to the assembly on the conduct of the common policies.

questions.stem: A card in tonight's pack explains that the treaty's text gave the project's institutions what?

options.text: The power to appoint and dismiss the governments of the member states.
The power to set the domestic tax rates of each member state.
The power to apply common rules directly and to account publicly for what they did.
The power to issue binding trade rules for parties outside the project.
options.misconception: confuses internal rules with external ones

questions.explanation: The clauses gave the institutions power of application and of accounting: they applied the common rules, published their decisions, submitted the accounts to an audit and reported to the assembly. Nothing in the note gave them control of taxes, governments or outside trade.
questions.hint: Look at the instructions to the executive.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a regional project appears
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a regional project changed the position of its members in the wider world.

stimulus.body: A position note records that the members of a regional project continued to be counted individually by the organisation of the wider world, that they kept their own armies and their own foreign ministries, and that they nevertheless found that a common representative in trade discussions was listened to where individual representatives had not been.

questions.stem: The study group's timeline notes that after the superpower's end, some members found they could speak with more weight; what did the note show?

options.text: That they had given up their own foreign ministries in favour of a common one.
options.misconception: claims the foreign ministries were pooled

options.text: That they had surrendered their separate representation in the wider organisation entirely.
That the wider organisation began to treat the group as a single member for voting.
That speaking together in some forums compensated for the small size of each member.

questions.explanation: The note shows that separate representation was retained while joint speaking in trade discussions carried more weight than separate speaking had. Membership of the wider organisation was unchanged and the foreign ministries stayed national.
questions.hint: Compare the two ways the members were heard.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule set aside inside a regional project
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise what setting aside a rule inside the regional project achieved.
questions.stem: The revision's closing question asks what setting aside a rule achieved for the regional project; which summary is best?

options.text: It dismantled the rule entirely, so that the project had no binding rules left at all.
options.misconception: claims the project was left without rules

options.text: It removed a barrier to action while leaving the project's overall direction and its institutions intact.
It transferred the rule's content to the member governments, which then applied it in their own way.
options.misconception: claims the rule was devolved to members

options.text: It postponed the question of the rule until the members had reached a new agreement on it.
options.misconception: claims the matter was merely postponed

questions.explanation: Setting a rule aside removed the specific barrier that had blocked action, whether unanimity or the composition of a body, while leaving the institutions and the project's direction intact. The other options describe a dismantling, a devolution or a delay that never happened.
questions.hint: Separate what changed from what stayed.
